title: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
summary: How an OS virtualizes the CPU (traps, timer interrupts, scheduling) and memory (paging, TLBs), why shared data needs locks, and how file systems survive crashes, with OSTEP's own worked examples.
outcomes: Explain how traps, the trap table and the timer interrupt let an OS run programs directly yet keep control
Compute turnaround and response time for FIFO, SJF, STCF and round robin schedules
Translate a virtual address through a page table and compute TLB hit rates for an access pattern
Explain why x++ on shared data races and why locks need atomic instructions such as test-and-set
Compute disk I/O time and explain how journaling makes multi-block updates crash-safe

blocks.md: An operating system (OS) has three jobs, which OSTEP calls the three easy pieces: **virtualization** (make one CPU and one memory look like many private ones), **concurrency** (let many things happen at once without corrupting shared data) and **persistence** (keep data safe on disks across crashes). This course walks through one core mechanism from each piece, using the same examples as the book so you can read along.

The first abstraction is the **process**: a running program. Its state is its memory (the *address space*: code, heap, stack), its registers (including the program counter, PC, and stack pointer) and its open files. The OS keeps a per-process record of this state, often called a process control block (PCB), in a *process list*.

A process is always in one of three simplified states:

- **Running**: executing instructions on a CPU.
- **Ready**: could run, but the OS has chosen to run something else.
- **Blocked**: waiting for some event, such as a disk read finishing, so it cannot run yet.

Moving from ready to running is called being *scheduled*; running to ready is being *descheduled*.

blocks.title: Two processes moving through the state machine

scenes.caption: Time 1 to 3 (OSTEP Figure 4.4): Process0 (P0) runs on the single CPU while Process1 (P1) waits in Ready.
Time 4: P0 initiates an I/O and becomes Blocked. The CPU would sit idle, so the OS schedules P1 instead.
Time 7: the disk finishes and raises an interrupt. The OS moves P0 to Ready, not straight to Running: P1 keeps the CPU.
Time 9: P1 has finished, so P0 is scheduled and runs to completion at time 10. Overlapping P0's I/O with P1's computation kept the CPU busy.

blocks.md: UNIX creates processes with two calls. `fork()` makes an almost exact copy of the caller: same code, a private copy of memory and registers. The only difference is the return value: the parent gets the child's process ID (PID), the child gets 0. `exec()` then replaces the current program with a new one, and `wait()` lets a parent block until a child exits. A UNIX shell runs the commands you type with exactly this fork, exec, wait sequence.

blocks.title: Tracing fork() and wait() (OSTEP p2.c)

scenes.caption: One process (PID 29266) prints hello. So far nothing unusual.
fork() returns twice: once in the parent with the child's PID, once in the new child with 0. Two processes now run this same code.
Suppose the scheduler runs the parent first. It calls wait(NULL) and becomes Blocked until its child exits.
The child takes the rc == 0 branch, prints, and exits.
wait() returns the child's PID and the parent prints last. Without wait() either order could appear; with it the output is deterministic.

blocks.md: Now the core question: how does the OS run a process fast but stay in control? The fast part is **direct execution**: load the program and jump to `main()`, so it runs natively on the CPU. The *limited* part needs hardware help. The CPU has a **user mode**, where restricted operations such as I/O raise an exception, and a **kernel mode**, where the OS can do anything.

A program asks for a privileged service with a **system call**. The C library puts a system-call number in a register and executes a **trap** instruction, which raises the privilege level and jumps into the kernel. The program cannot pick the jump target: at boot the kernel installs a **trap table** telling the hardware which handler runs for each event. When the work is done, **return-from-trap** drops back to user mode.

That solves restricted operations, but not a process that loops forever and never makes a system call. The fix is a **timer interrupt**: a device, started by the OS at boot, that interrupts the CPU every few milliseconds and runs an OS handler. At that point the OS can do a **context switch**: save the current process's registers and restore another's.

blocks.title: Limited direct execution with a timer interrupt

scenes.caption: At boot, in kernel mode, the OS tells the hardware where its trap handlers live and starts the interrupt timer. Both are privileged operations.
Process A runs directly on the CPU in user mode. The OS is not running at all, so it cannot act until something hands control back.

add.label: user mode, jump to A's PC

scenes.caption: The timer fires. Hardware saves A's registers onto A's kernel stack, switches to kernel mode and jumps to the timer handler.
The scheduler picks B. switch() saves A's kernel registers into A's process structure, restores B's, and switches to B's kernel stack.
return-from-trap now restores B's registers, because the stack it pops from is B's. The CPU drops to user mode and resumes B where it left off.
Later B makes a system call. It traps into the handler chosen at boot, the OS does the work, and return-from-trap resumes B after the trap.

blocks.md: Limited direct execution: let the program run natively, but first set up the hardware (trap table, timer, user mode) so that the OS always gets control back. A system call is the voluntary way back in; the timer interrupt is the involuntary one.

A system call is not just a function call. It looks like one because the C library wraps it, but inside is a trap that changes privilege level, and the kernel, not the caller, decides which code runs.

blocks.question: Under a purely cooperative OS (no timer interrupt), a process enters `while (1) {}` and never makes a system call. What happens?
options: The OS never runs again on that CPU; in practice the machine must be rebooted
The OS notices after one time slice and preempts it
The trap table automatically jumps to the scheduler after a while
The process is killed because infinite loops are privileged operations
blocks.explain: With no timer interrupt, the OS only regains control when the process makes a system call or does something illegal. An infinite loop does neither, so the OS cannot run. OSTEP notes the only recourse is to reboot. This is exactly why the timer interrupt exists.

blocks.question: Why must the instruction that installs the trap table be privileged?
options: Because it is slow and should run only at boot
Because the trap table is stored on disk
Because a user process could otherwise point system calls and interrupts at its own code and take over the machine
Because user programs do not know the system-call numbers
blocks.explain: The trap table decides which code runs in kernel mode on every trap and interrupt. If a user program could install its own, it would run arbitrary code with full privilege, defeating all protection. So, like starting the timer, it is restricted to kernel mode.

lessons.title: CPU scheduling: turnaround time versus response time

blocks.md: The timer gives the OS a chance to switch processes; the **scheduler** decides *which* one runs. To compare policies we need metrics. **Turnaround time** is completion time minus arrival time; it matters for batch jobs. **Response time** is the time from arrival to the first time the job runs; it matters for interactive programs.

blocks.tex: T_{\text{turnaround}} = T_{\text{completion}} - T_{\text{arrival}} \qquad T_{\text{response}} = T_{\text{firstrun}} - T_{\text{arrival}}

blocks.md: OSTEP's running example: three jobs A, B and C arrive at time 0. A needs 100 seconds of CPU, B and C need 10 each. **FIFO** (first in, first out) runs them in arrival order, A first. **SJF** (shortest job first) runs the shortest first. Both are non-preemptive: once started, a job runs to completion.

blocks.prompt: Under FIFO, with A (100 s) arriving just before B and C (10 s each), what is the average turnaround time? And under SJF?
blocks.reveal: FIFO: A finishes at 100, B at 110, C at 120, so the average is $(100+110+120)/3 = 110$ s. SJF runs B and C first: they finish at 10 and 20, A at 120, so the average is $(10+20+120)/3 = 50$ s. Same work, less than half the average wait. Short jobs stuck behind a long one is called the **convoy effect**.

blocks.title: FIFO, SJF and STCF on the same three jobs

scenes.caption: FIFO, all arrive at 0: A hogs the CPU for 100 s. Turnaround: A 100, B 110, C 120, average 110 s.
SJF, all arrive at 0: B and C go first. Turnaround: B 10, C 20, A 120, average 50 s. With simultaneous arrivals SJF is optimal for average turnaround.
Now B and C arrive at t = 10, after A started. Non-preemptive SJF cannot stop A. Turnaround: A 100, B 100, C 110, average 103.33 s. The convoy is back.
STCF (preemptive SJF): at t = 10 it preempts A, whose 90 s remaining is longest. Turnaround: A 120, B 10, C 20, average 50 s. Response: 0, 0, 10, average 3.33 s.

blocks.md: **STCF** (shortest time-to-completion first) adds preemption: whenever a job arrives, run whichever job has the least time *remaining*. It needs the timer and context switch from lesson 1. But all these policies are bad for response time: if three 5-second jobs arrive together, SJF makes the third wait 10 seconds before it runs even once.

**Round robin (RR)** fixes response time: run each job for a **time slice** (also called a quantum), then switch to the next job in the queue. The slice must be a multiple of the timer-interrupt period, so with a 10 ms timer it could be 10, 20 or 30 ms.

blocks.title: SJF versus round robin on three 5-second jobs

scenes.caption: SJF (ties broken A, B, C): response times 0, 5, 10 (average 5 s); turnaround 5, 10, 15 (average 10 s).
RR with a 1 s slice: every job starts within 2 s, so average response is 1 s. But A finishes at 13, B at 14, C at 15: average turnaround 14 s, worse than SJF's 10.

blocks.md: Each switch costs time: saving and restoring registers, plus colder CPU caches, TLB and branch predictors for the incoming job. OSTEP's example: with a 1 ms switch cost, a 10 ms slice wastes roughly 10% of the CPU, and a 100 ms slice under 1%. The plot below uses the simple model overhead $= c/(q+c)$ for switch cost $c$ and slice $q$.

scenes.caption: With c = 1 ms, a 10 ms slice loses about 9% to switching and a 100 ms slice about 1%. Longer slices amortize the fixed cost.
Simplified model: real switch costs also include refilling caches and the TLB. If the effective cost rises to 3 ms, short slices become very expensive.

blocks.md:
Real schedulers do not know job lengths. OSTEP's answer is the **multi-level feedback queue (MLFQ)**, which learns from behavior:

1. Higher priority runs first; equal priorities share the CPU round robin.
2. New jobs start at the top priority (assume a job is short and interactive).
3. Once a job uses up its time allotment at a level, it moves down one level, no matter how many times it gave up the CPU.
4. Every period S, move all jobs back to the top, so long jobs do not starve.

OSTEP notes that BSD UNIX derivatives, Solaris and Windows NT and later use forms of MLFQ as their base scheduler.

No policy wins on every metric. SJF and STCF minimize average turnaround but give long waits before a job first runs; round robin gives fast response but stretches every job's completion. Choosing a scheduler means choosing which metric you care about.

blocks.question: Three 5-second jobs arrive together. You switch from SJF to round robin with a 1 s slice. What happens to average turnaround and average response time?
options: Both improve
Turnaround gets worse (10 s to 14 s) and response gets better (5 s to 1 s)
Turnaround improves and response gets worse
Both stay the same because the total work is unchanged
blocks.explain: RR starts every job almost immediately, so average response drops from 5 s to 1 s. But it interleaves the jobs, so all of them finish near the end: 13, 14 and 15 s, averaging 14 s versus SJF's 10 s. Fairness over short time scales costs turnaround.

blocks.question: A job in MLFQ runs for 9 ms of a 10 ms allotment, then issues a tiny I/O, and repeats forever. Under the final rule (allotment counts total use at a level), what happens?
options: It stays at top priority forever because it always yields before its allotment ends
It is demoted once its total CPU use at that level reaches the allotment, even across many short bursts
It is killed for gaming the scheduler
It is promoted because it does I/O
blocks.explain: An older version of the rule reset the allotment whenever a job gave up the CPU, so this pattern could monopolize the CPU. The refined allotment rule (item 3 in the list above, Rule 4 in OSTEP) tracks total time used at a level, whether in one long burst or many short ones, so the gaming job is demoted.

lessons.title: Virtual memory: paging, page tables and the TLB

blocks.md: The second thing the OS virtualizes is memory. Every process sees its own **address space** starting at 0, and every pointer you used in C is a **virtual address**. The hardware's memory management unit (MMU) translates each one into a **physical address** on every load, store and instruction fetch. This gives isolation (a process cannot even name another's memory) and lets the OS place memory wherever it likes.

**Paging** chops the address space into fixed-size **pages** and physical memory into same-size **page frames**. A per-process **page table** maps each virtual page number (VPN) to a physical frame number (PFN). The low bits of an address, the **offset**, select a byte inside the page and are never translated.

OSTEP's tiny example: a 64-byte address space with 16-byte pages, so 4 virtual pages and 6-bit addresses (2 VPN bits, 4 offset bits). Physical memory is 128 bytes (8 frames, 7-bit addresses). The page table maps VP 0 to frame 3, VP 1 to frame 7, VP 2 to frame 5 and VP 3 to frame 2. Now translate the load `movl 21, %eax`.

blocks.title: Translating virtual address 21 to physical address 117

scenes.caption: 21 in binary is 010101. With 16-byte pages, the low 4 bits are the offset and the top 2 bits are the VPN.
VPN = 01 = 1 and offset = 0101 = 5: byte 5 of virtual page 1. The hardware indexes the page table with the VPN.
The entry says frame 7 (binary 111). Replace the VPN with the PFN; the offset bits are copied unchanged.
Physical address 1110101 = 7 x 16 + 5 = 117. Same offset, different page: that is all translation does.

blocks.md: Each **page table entry (PTE)** holds the PFN plus bits the OS and hardware use: a **valid** bit (unused regions of a sparse address space are invalid, and touching them traps to the OS), **protection** bits (read, write, execute), a **present** bit (in memory or swapped to disk), a **dirty** bit and a **reference** (accessed) bit. On x86 the present bit doubles as valid, and the U/S bit decides whether user mode may touch the page.

blocks.prompt: A 32-bit address space with 4 KB pages and 4-byte PTEs uses a simple linear (array) page table. How big is one process's page table? And for 100 processes?
blocks.reveal: 4 KB pages need 12 offset bits, leaving a 20-bit VPN, so $2^{20}$ entries (about a million). At 4 bytes each that is $2^{20} \times 4 = 4$ MB per process, and 400 MB for 100 processes, just for translations. This is why real systems use **multi-level page tables**, below.

blocks.caption: One entry per possible virtual page, valid or not.

blocks.md: A **multi-level page table** chops the linear table into page-sized pieces and adds a **page directory** that points to them. If a whole piece holds only invalid entries, it is simply not allocated. Space now grows with the memory a process actually uses. The price: whenever a translation must be read from the page table, the hardware needs two memory loads (directory, then PTE) instead of one. x86 uses this kind of tree, and the hardware finds its root through the CR3 register.

Paging has a speed problem too: every access first needs a PTE from memory. The fix is a **translation lookaside buffer (TLB)**, a small, fast hardware cache of recent VPN to PFN translations inside the MMU. On a **TLB hit** translation is nearly free; on a **TLB miss** the page table is consulted (by the hardware on x86, or by an OS trap handler on software-managed TLBs such as MIPS) and the TLB is filled.

blocks.title: TLB hits while summing a 10-integer array

scenes.caption: OSTEP's setup: 4-byte ints starting at virtual address 100, 8-bit addresses, 16-byte pages (VPN = address / 16). The TLB starts empty.
a[0] at address 100 is on VPN 6: miss, the page table is walked and the TLB filled. a[1] and a[2] are on the same page: hits.
a[3] at 112 starts VPN 7: one miss, then a[4] to a[6] hit.
a[7] at 128 starts VPN 8: miss, then two hits. Total 7 hits out of 10: a 70% hit rate on the very first pass, thanks to spatial locality.
Loop over the array again soon after: if the TLB still holds VPNs 6, 7 and 8, all 10 accesses hit. That is temporal locality.

blocks.md: Bigger pages mean fewer TLB misses for dense data: with 32-byte pages the same loop would miss less, and with typical 4 KB pages a sequential scan misses only once per page. Programs that jump randomly across many pages are the ones that suffer.
The offset is never translated, and the page table is per process. Two processes can use the same virtual address 21 and reach completely different physical bytes; that is the isolation, not a bug.

blocks.question: Using the same 64-byte address space and page table (VP 0 to frame 3, VP 1 to 7, VP 2 to 5, VP 3 to 2), what physical address does virtual address 40 map to?
blocks.explain: 40 is 101000 in binary: VPN 10 = 2 and offset 1000 = 8. VP 2 lives in frame 5, so the physical address is 5 x 16 + 8 = 88. Answer 40 forgets translation; 72 would be frame 4; 117 is the earlier example.

blocks.question: Why does a multi-level page table make a TLB miss more expensive than a linear page table?
options: The TLB must be flushed after each lookup
The walk needs a load from the page directory and then from the page of PTEs, instead of one load
Multi-level tables are stored on disk
Each level must be translated by the TLB first
blocks.explain: A linear table needs one memory reference to fetch the PTE. A two-level table first reads the page directory entry to find the right page of the page table, then reads the PTE: two loads. It is a time-space trade-off; on a TLB hit the cost is identical.

blocks.md: A **thread** is a second point of execution inside the same process. Each thread has its own registers, program counter and stack, but all threads share one address space, so they see the same globals and heap. Switching between threads works like a process context switch (state is saved in a thread control block), except the page table stays the same.
OSTEP's first threaded program starts two threads, each adding 1 to a shared global `counter` ten million times. The expected result is 20,000,000.

blocks.prompt: What do you expect when you run it, even on a single CPU?
blocks.reveal: Sometimes 20000000. But OSTEP's runs also printed **19345221** and then **19221041**: wrong, and different every time. Updates were lost. The outcome depends on exactly when the timer interrupt switched threads, which makes the result **indeterminate**.

blocks.md: The C statement `counter = counter + 1` is not one machine step. The compiler emits three x86 instructions: load the value into register `eax`, add one to the register, store the register back. A timer interrupt can arrive between any two of them, and each thread has its own saved copy of `eax`.

blocks.title: How one increment gets lost (OSTEP Figure 26.7)

scenes.caption: Thread 1 loads counter (50) into its eax.
Thread 1 adds one: its eax is 51. Then the timer fires; the OS saves T1's registers, including eax = 51, and switches to Thread 2.
Thread 2 runs all three instructions: it loads 50, adds one, and stores 51. Memory now holds 51.
Another interrupt resumes Thread 1 at its third instruction. It stores its stale eax = 51 into memory.
Two increments ran, but counter went from 50 to 51, not 52. Repeat this millions of times and you get 19,345,221 instead of 20,000,000.

blocks.md: This is a **race condition** (here, a data race): the result depends on the timing of execution. Code that touches shared data and must not run in more than one thread at once is a **critical section**. What we want is **mutual exclusion**: while one thread is inside, others are kept out. Dijkstra coined virtually all of these terms; his 1968 paper *Cooperating Sequential Processes* describes the problem clearly.
The tool for mutual exclusion is a **lock**. With POSIX threads you wrap the critical section:

blocks.caption: Only the thread holding the lock may run the increment, so the three instructions can no longer interleave.

blocks.md: How would you build `lock()` yourself? A first try uses a plain `flag` variable: spin while `flag == 1`, then set `flag = 1`. This fails for the same reason the counter did: the *test* and the *set* are separate steps, and an interrupt can land between them.

blocks.title: A lock built from a plain flag lets both threads in

scenes.caption: flag starts at 0. Thread 1 calls lock() and tests the flag: it is 0, so T1 will fall out of the loop.
An interrupt switches to Thread 2 before T1 sets the flag. T2 also sees flag == 0 and sets it to 1. T2 is in the critical section.
T1 resumes at line 4 and sets flag = 1 too. Both threads are now inside the critical section: no mutual exclusion.

blocks.md: Hardware fixes this with an atomic instruction. **Test-and-set** (atomic exchange; `xchg` on x86) writes a new value and returns the old one as a single, indivisible step. A lock becomes: keep calling `TestAndSet(&flag, 1)` until it returns 0. Whoever sees 0 is the one thread that flipped the flag from free to held.

blocks.caption: OSTEP's spin lock (Figure 28.3). The C function only describes the semantics; real code uses the CPU's atomic instruction.

blocks.md: This **spin lock** is correct but not fair (a waiter may spin forever), and on one CPU it can waste a lot: if the holder is preempted, each of the other N - 1 threads may spin away a whole time slice. Real locks therefore sleep instead of spinning when contended. Linux provides the **futex** system call for this: `futex_wait` puts the caller to sleep if a memory word still has an expected value, and `futex_wake` wakes a waiter.

Any read-modify-write of shared data (even `x++`) is several instructions, and a context switch can split them. Protect every critical section with a lock, and build locks on atomic hardware instructions, never on plain loads and stores.
"It is a single line of C" does not make it atomic, and `volatile` does not either. OSTEP's counter is declared `volatile int` and still loses updates.

blocks.question: Why does the flag-based lock fail while the test-and-set lock works?
options: Test-and-set is faster, so the window for an interrupt is smaller
The flag lock forgets to reset the flag in unlock()
The flag lock only fails on multiprocessors
Test-and-set reads the old value and writes the new one as one atomic step, so two threads cannot both see the lock as free
blocks.explain: In the flag lock, a thread can test (see 0) and then be preempted before it sets the flag, letting another thread also see 0. Test-and-set fuses test and set into a single atomic operation. Speed has nothing to do with it, and the failure happens even on one CPU with a timer interrupt.

blocks.question: On a single CPU with a non-preemptive scheduler (no timer switches), Thread 2 calls a spin lock held by Thread 1. What happens?
options: Thread 2 acquires the lock after one time slice
Thread 2 spins forever: Thread 1 never gets the CPU back to release the lock
The lock automatically turns into a sleeping lock
Thread 1 releases the lock because spinning causes an interrupt
blocks.explain: A spinning thread never gives up the CPU on its own. Without preemption, the holder never runs again, so the lock is never released. OSTEP points out that spin locks need a preemptive scheduler to work correctly on a single processor.

lessons.title: Persistence: disks, inodes and crash-safe journaling

blocks.md: The third piece is keeping data across power loss. On a hard disk drive (HDD), reading a random block takes three steps: **seek** (move the arm to the right track), **rotation** (wait for the sector to spin under the head) and **transfer** (read the bits).

OSTEP compares two Seagate drives. The Cheetah 15K.5 spins at 15,000 RPM, seeks in 4 ms on average and transfers at up to 125 MB/s. The Barracuda spins at 7,200 RPM, seeks in 9 ms and transfers at 105 MB/s. Average rotational delay is half a rotation: $60000/15000/2 = 2$ ms for the Cheetah and $60000/7200/2 \approx 4.17$ ms for the Barracuda.

blocks.prompt: For a random 4 KB read on the Cheetah: seek 4 ms, rotation 2 ms, transfer $0.004\ \text{MB} / 125\ \text{MB/s} = 0.032$ ms. What throughput does that give?
blocks.reveal: $T_{I/O} = 6.032$ ms, so $R_{I/O} = 0.004\ \text{MB} / 6.032\ \text{ms} \approx 0.66$ MB/s, about 0.5% of the drive's 125 MB/s peak. Almost all the time is mechanical positioning. The Barracuda is worse: 13.2 ms per read, about 0.30 MB/s (OSTEP rounds to 0.31).

blocks.title: Random 4 KB reads versus one sequential 100 MB read

scenes.caption: Random 4 KB reads: 0.66 and 0.30 MB/s. Each tiny read pays a full seek plus half a rotation.
Sequential 100 MB: one seek and rotation, then 800 ms (Cheetah) or 952 ms (Barracuda) of transfer. Totals 806 and 966 ms give 124.1 and 103.6 MB/s.
The ratio is about 187x for the Cheetah and 342x for the Barracuda. Hence OSTEP's tip: use disks sequentially, or at least in large chunks.

blocks.title: Disk throughput as the request size grows

scenes.caption: Cheetah model (4 ms seek, 2 ms rotation, 125 MB/s). Throughput only approaches the peak once each request is megabytes long, so positioning cost is amortized.
Barracuda model (9 ms seek, 4.17 ms rotation, 105 MB/s). Slower positioning pushes the curve right: you need even bigger requests. Simplified: ignores caches and request scheduling.

blocks.md: A **file system** organizes the disk into blocks. OSTEP's very simple file system (vsfs) uses 64 blocks of 4 KB: block 0 is the **superblock** (sizes, where things are, a magic number), block 1 the **inode bitmap**, block 2 the **data bitmap** (one bit per object: free or in use), blocks 3 to 7 the **inode table**, and blocks 8 to 63 the 56 data blocks.

An **inode** (index node) holds a file's metadata: type, size, owner, permissions, timestamps and pointers to its data blocks. Files are named internally by their **inode number**, and the inode's location is pure arithmetic. With 256-byte inodes, a 4 KB block holds 16, so five blocks give 80 inodes.

scenes.caption: The first 12 of 64 blocks. The inode table starts at block 3, byte address 12 KB.
Offset of inode 32 inside the table: 32 x 256 = 8192 bytes = 8 KB, which is inode-table block 8192 / 4096 = 2.
Byte address 12 KB + 8 KB = 20 KB, disk block 5. Disks address 512-byte sectors, so the file system reads sector 20 x 1024 / 512 = 40.
That 4 KB block holds inodes 32 to 47; inode 32 is the first 256 bytes of it.

blocks.md:
Now the **crash-consistency problem**. Appending one block to a file requires three separate writes: the updated inode `I[v2]` (new size, new pointer), the updated data bitmap `B[v2]` and the data block `Db`. The disk commits one write at a time, so a crash can leave any subset on disk:

- Only `Db`: harmless for consistency, just lost data.
- Only `I[v2]`: the inode points at garbage, and disagrees with the bitmap.
- Only `B[v2]`: a block marked used that nothing points to, a space leak.
- `I[v2]` and `B[v2]` but not `Db`: metadata is consistent, but the file contains garbage.

Early file systems ran **fsck** after a crash, which scans the entire disk to repair inconsistencies: correct, but slow on large disks. **Journaling** (write-ahead logging), used by Linux ext3 and ext4, writes a note describing the update to a log area first. If a crash hits mid-update, recovery reads only the small log.

blocks.title: Data journaling, then where a crash lands

scenes.caption: 1. Journal write: TxB (begin, with a transaction ID), I[v2], B[v2] and Db go to the log; they may be issued together. Wait for them to complete.
2. Journal commit: only then write TxE. It fits in one 512-byte sector, which the disk writes atomically, so the transaction is either committed or not.
3. Checkpoint: write I[v2], B[v2] and Db to their real locations. 4. Free: later, mark the transaction reusable in the journal superblock.
Crash before TxE is on disk: recovery sees no committed transaction and skips it. The file system is in its old, consistent state.
Crash during checkpoint: the log holds a committed transaction, so recovery replays it (redo logging). Rewriting blocks that already landed is harmless.
Ordered (metadata) journaling, as in ext3's ordered mode: write Db to its final place first, then journal only TxB, I[v2], B[v2] and TxE. Data is written once, and a pointer never points at garbage.

blocks.md: Write the pointed-to object before the object that points to it, and make the commit a single atomic write. Journaling turns three unordered writes into one all-or-nothing transaction, and recovery only has to read the log, not the whole disk.
Data journaling writes every data block twice, which halves sequential write bandwidth. That is why metadata (ordered) journaling is the more common choice; OSTEP notes NTFS and XFS use forms of it.

blocks.question: A crash leaves only the new inode I[v2] on disk; the bitmap B[v2] and data block Db were not written. What is the state?
options: Inconsistent: the inode points to a block the bitmap says is free, and that block holds old garbage
Consistent and correct: the inode is the source of truth
A harmless space leak
Lost data but a consistent file system
blocks.explain: The inode now points to the new data block (block 5 in OSTEP), but Db never reached it, so reading the file returns whatever was there before. The bitmap still says that block is free, contradicting the inode. This is the case fsck or journaling exists to prevent. Only-Db is the harmless case; only-bitmap is the leak.

blocks.question: In data journaling, why must the file system wait for TxB, I[v2], B[v2] and Db to finish before writing TxE, instead of issuing all five writes at once?
options: Because the disk can only accept one write at a time
Because TxE must be written to the final location, not the journal
Because the disk may reorder a large write; TxE could land before Db, and replay would then copy garbage as if it were committed
Because waiting makes the journal smaller
blocks.explain: Disks schedule writes internally. If all five are issued together, TxE might hit the disk while Db has not. After a crash the transaction looks committed, and recovery would checkpoint garbage. Writing TxE only after the rest completes, as an atomic 512-byte write, closes the window.
